slides.text: Train/test split: why we hide data from the model
slides.say: Data Science from Scratch, lesson eighteen: the train test split, and why we hide data from the model.

slides.text: A model can memorise the data it learned from
slides.sub: Great scores on old data ≠ good on new data
slides.say: A model can do very well on the data it learned from, partly by memorising it. That tells you little about how it will do on new data, which is the whole point.

slides.text:
Training set: the model learns
Test set: kept hidden
slides.sub: Score the model only on the test set
slides.say: The fix is simple. Split your data in two. The model learns from the training set, and the test set stays hidden until the end, when you use it to score the model.

slides.sub: A common rule of thumb, not a law
slides.say: A common choice is eighty percent for training and twenty for testing, or seventy and thirty. These are rules of thumb, not laws.

slides.text: Stratify: keep the same fraud rate in both sets
slides.sub: Otherwise the test set may have almost no fraud
slides.say: With rare events like fraud, a random split can leave the test set with very few fraud cases. Stratifying keeps the share of fraud roughly the same in both sets.

slides.text: Train on the past, test on the future
slides.sub: For data that changes over time, split by date
slides.say: When data changes over time, as fraud patterns often do, it's usually better to split by date. Train on older data and test on newer data, just like the model will face in real life.

slides.text: Never let the model see the test set while it learns.
slides.say: So the takeaway: keep the test set hidden while the model learns, or your scores will look better than reality.

summary: Split data into a training set the model learns from and a hidden test set used only to score it, often around 80/20 or 70/30. Stratify for rare events like fraud, and split by date when data changes over time.
practice: You have 1,000 past transactions, 20 of them fraud, from January to December. Write down how you would split them into training and test sets, and explain why a random split could mislead you.
